A favorite optimistic view of the future of AI is from a pessimistic book that not about AI: "Rise and Fall of American Growth," which argues that we had a one-time explosion in living standards from 1870 and 1920 (& later outside the US). In 1870: no toilets, no city plumbing, lamp light, no central heating, little public health, horses for local travel, etc. In 50 years, all of this was solved & the nation was electrified. In the next fifty modern medicine, air travel and telecommunication happened. The book then points out that we have had no changes in lifestyle of similar scale since the 1970s. Written in 2016, it argued that we would likely never experience another boom like the "Special Century." The positive view of AI should make us ask "But what if we do?" and "How do we make it all go right?"

It isn't that weird to think that "this time is different" - we had a couple of Industrial Revolutions over the past couple centuries, just because we got used to a relatively steady-state regime post World War Two with a regular pace of growth doesn't mean it continues forever. Across our projects @GoogleDeepMind, we are witnessing a genuine phase transition in the pace of scientific discovery. You will see a glimpse of this in our releases in the next few weeks.

Elon Musk explains one of the most terrifying existential threats humanity faces: a massive comet striking Earth and potentially wiping out civilization “Earth does not currently have any ability to stop asteroids. Now with Starship, we then have some ability to stop an asteroid actually, technically, a comet would be the real danger Because there are billions, if not more than billions, maybe trillions of objects that are in the outer solar system, with very long-period comets An example that most people are probably aware of is Halley’s Comet. It’s slightly under once per century that Halley’s Comet comes by. Many comets have very long periods that we simply don’t know exist And for example, the comet Shoemaker-Levy when that hit Jupiter, it made a hole in Jupiter the size of Earth. So if that did hit Earth, game over "Everything’s dead" So there’s always some risk of such a thing occurring, and the probable lifespan of life is just much greater if we’re a multi-planet and ultimately multi-stellar civilization” https://x.com/XFreeze/status/2022644681247695041/video/1 Media

The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people. This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production. Seriously. It’s incomparable. But cars are going to become robots, their forms and functions will change, and we won’t be coming back to this moment. Get it while you can.

In 2014, Elon Musk started a school called Ad Astra inside SpaceX headquarters to teach kids to think from first principles. In rare footage, he walks them through it: "Let's look at the physics and economics of a rocket..." The method: don't accept that something is impossible because others failed at it. Break the problem down to what physics and materials actually allow, then reason up from there. It's the same thinking that made reusable rockets real at SpaceX.
